presentingComplaint: 10 days of worsening loss of appetite, nausea and darkening urine, with yellow eyes noticed by family over the last 4 days
history: Frail 74-year-old woman, lives with her son's family, previously independent in basic activities but slowed over the past year. Ten days ago she developed vague malaise, poor appetite and low-grade fever with body aches, which the family attributed to 'weakness'. Over the last 4-5 days her urine turned dark (tea-coloured), stools became pale, and relatives noticed scleral icterus. She reports mild dull right upper abdominal discomfort and generalised itching but no severe pain, no rigors and no biliary-type colic. No prior liver disease, no gallstones, no jaundice in the past. Teetotaller. No paracetamol overdose, no new prescription drugs, no herbal/ayurvedic remedies, no anti-tubercular therapy. Regular medications limited to amlodipine and calcium. Lives in a semi-urban area with intermittent municipal water supply; a neighbour reportedly had 'jaundice' a few weeks earlier. No recent travel outside India, no blood transfusion, no invasive procedures. Family notes she has become more forgetful and drowsy in the last 2 days.
examination: Frail, thin, deeply icteric elderly woman, alert but slow to respond with mild inattention on cognitive testing; no gross flap elicited. Well hydrated. Scratch marks over limbs. Abdomen soft, mild tender smooth hepatomegaly ~3 cm below costal margin, no splenomegaly clinically appreciable, no ascites, no shifting dullness, no palpable gallbladder, Murphy negative. No spider naevi, no palmar erythema, no caput medusae, no asterixis at rest. No peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease.
imaging: USG abdomen: mildly enlarged liver with normal, homogeneous echotexture; smooth capsule; no focal lesion; gallbladder normal with mildly oedematous wall and no calculi; common bile duct and intrahepatic ducts NOT dilated; portal vein patent with normal calibre; spleen upper-normal size; no ascites; no features of chronic liver disease/cirrhosis.
microbiology: Anti-HEV IgM POSITIVE; HEV RNA detected by PCR. Anti-HAV IgM negative. HBsAg negative, IgM anti-HBc negative. Anti-HCV negative. Leptospira IgM negative. Dengue NS1/IgM negative. Blood cultures sterile.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute viral hepatitis E (elderly, waterborne, more severe course) - most consistent
Drug-induced / toxic hepatitis (excluded: no hepatotoxin exposure)
Acute cholangitis / biliary obstruction (excluded: no ductal dilatation, no rigors, transaminase-predominant pattern)
Leptospirosis (excluded: negative serology, no conjunctival suffusion/renal failure)
Decompensated chronic liver disease (excluded: no chronic-liver stigmata, normal liver architecture on USG)
finalDiagnosis: Acute viral hepatitis E with early hepatic dysfunction (borderline INR and subtle encephalopathy) in a frail elderly woman - hepatocellular pattern, no biliary obstruction
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Acute Viral Hepatitis
EASL - Clinical Practice Guidelines on Hepatitis E Virus Infection - 2018
stewardship: Acute viral hepatitis is a self-limiting viral illness; empiric antibacterial therapy is NOT indicated and should be avoided. Management is supportive: rest, adequate nutrition/hydration, antiemetics, avoidance of hepatotoxins and sedatives. Because elderly patients with hepatitis E have a higher risk of severe/fulminant course, monitor INR, bilirubin and mental status closely for acute liver failure and involve hepatology early; ribavirin is reserved for chronic HEV in the immunosuppressed, not acute infection in an immunocompetent host. Antibiotics only if a superimposed bacterial infection (e.g., SBP, sepsis) is objectively documented.
contraindications: Avoid paracetamol at high dose and other hepatotoxic drugs
Avoid sedatives/benzodiazepines which may precipitate/mask encephalopathy
edgeCases: Elderly and pregnant patients with hepatitis E have markedly higher mortality and risk of acute liver failure
Cholestatic variant can cause prolonged jaundice and pruritus, mimicking biliary obstruction
Subtle encephalopathy in the frail elderly may be mistaken for delirium or dementia
expectedMaiK: Elderly frail woman with subacute painless jaundice, dark urine, markedly elevated transaminases in a hepatocellular pattern, no biliary dilatation on USG, and positive anti-HEV IgM/HEV RNA - acute viral hepatitis E. Recognise the higher risk of acute liver failure in the elderly and that antibiotics are not indicated.

expectedInvestigations: Liver function tests (AST/ALT, bilirubin fractions, ALP/GGT, albumin)
INR / prothrombin time (assess synthetic function and ALF risk)
Viral hepatitis serology (anti-HEV IgM, anti-HAV IgM, HBsAg/IgM anti-HBc, anti-HCV)
USG abdomen to exclude biliary obstruction and chronic liver disease
Serum ammonia and bedside cognitive assessment for encephalopathy

investigations: Acute viral hepatitis serology (anti-HEV IgM, anti-HAV IgM, HBsAg, anti-HCV)

regressionAssertions: No antibacterial antibiotics should be recommended (viral, self-limiting)
Hepatocellular pattern (ALT/AST in thousands) with non-dilated biliary tree must steer away from CHOLANGITIS
Positive anti-HEV IgM/HEV RNA with negative other viral markers confirms hepatitis E
Elderly host with raised INR and subtle encephalopathy must trigger monitoring for acute liver failure
